title: The Morning After Naraka
tease: He asks for one thing as he dies: that the day be kept as a festival rather than as his defeat. He gets it, and people still keep it.

source.traditionNote: The Bhāgavata gives the war, Satyabhāmā's hand and the women brought out of his house. The dying request — lamps rather than mourning — is the festival's own story. It is why the fourteenth of the dark fortnight is called Naraka Chaturdaśī, and why in the south that day, not the new moon after it, is Deepavali.
checkedAgainst: Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Skandha 10 — Tagare trans. (Motilal Banarsidass)

sourcing.claim: Naraka rules Prāgjyotiṣa and has taken what belongs to others, including Aditi's earrings
Prāgjyotiṣa is ringed with defences — hills, water, fire, wind, and a net of nooses
Kṛṣṇa cuts through the fortifications before reaching the city
The kingdom is given to Naraka's son at his mother's asking
The earrings are returned to Aditi
Kṛṣṇa goes against him with Satyabhāmā
Satyabhāmā is on the field and it is her hand at the end
sourcing.locus: Bhāgavata 10.59; and the tradition that follows it

sourcing.claim: Sixteen thousand one hundred women are found held in his house and are freed
Kṛṣṇa marries them rather than leave them unplaceable in that society
Naraka's mother is the earth, and she asks for his son to be spared
The dying request that the day be a festival is tradition, not a verse of the Bhāgavata

variants.tellings: The Bhāgavata puts Satyabhāmā on the field and the tradition around it is firm that she strikes the blow, because a boon protected Naraka from Kṛṣṇa. Some retellings quietly give the whole thing to Kṛṣṇa.
variants.weTell: Hers, because the text put her there and the reason is the interesting part.

variants.tellings: The Bhāgavata does not have it. It is the standard explanation of why the fourteenth night is lamps rather than mourning, and it is told everywhere the festival is kept.
variants.weTell: The request, marked as the festival's story rather than the book's.

audience.careNote: A war and a death, told at a distance — no wounds described. Two harder things sit in the middle of it: thousands of women were being held in his house against their will, said plainly and without detail, and the man who dies is somebody's son, and his mother is in the room. Both are the point rather than decoration.

values: the mercy nobody had to give
a villain who is not only that

blocks.text: «Narakāsura» had taken a great deal that was not his, and the last of it was a pair of earrings belonging to the mother of the gods.
So «Kṛṣṇa» went to get them back. And he did not go alone.
«Satyabhāmā» went with him, onto the field, which queens in these stories generally do not.
There was a reason. Naraka had a protection on him — he could not be brought down by Kṛṣṇa. Nobody had thought to include Kṛṣṇa's wife.
In the telling we are following, it was her hand at the end. That is why «Satyabhāmā» was on the field at all.
Then they went into his house, and found sixteen thousand women being kept there who did not want to be.

They were let out. Then came a harder question: where could sixteen thousand women go in a world that would not take them back? «Kṛṣṇa» married them. Here the marriage is not told as romance; it gave them a place and standing in that society.
And Naraka was somebody's son. His mother is the earth, and she was there, and she asked for his boy to be left alone, and she was listened to.

Later festival tradition remembers Naraka asking for something at the end: when people remembered this day — the fourteenth, the _chaturdaśī_ — they should not keep it only as the day he lost. They should light lamps and be glad.
His city had been ringed with hills and water and fire and a net of nooses, and all of it had to come apart before anyone could even see him. She stood in the same chariot for the whole of it.
Everyone remembers the lamps. Almost nobody remembers that the man they are for asked for them himself, on the worst day of his life.
«Narakāsura» had taken a great deal that was not his.
Kingdoms, mostly, and whatever was in them. The last thing on the list was a pair of earrings belonging to the mother of the gods, which is the sort of theft that gets noticed.
So «Kṛṣṇa» went to get them back.
And he did not go alone, which is the first surprising thing in this story.
«Satyabhāmā» went with him. Onto the field. Not to wave anybody off — into it, in the chariot, for the whole thing.

There was a reason, and it is a good one. Naraka had a protection on him: he could not be brought down by Kṛṣṇa. Somebody had been careful when they asked for that, and had thought of everything except a wife.
So it was her hand at the end.
That is the part most people have never been told, and it is why she was there at all. The story is not a husband's with a wife watching. It is hers, and he drove.
Getting to him was not simple. His city was built behind layer after layer of defence.

His city sat inside rings. Hills first, then water, then fire, then wind — and then, strung across everything, a net of nooses that tightened on whatever came through. Each ring had to be taken apart in turn before the next one was even visible.
That took a while, and the whole time she was standing in the same chariot, and neither of them left.
Then they went into his house.
And in it were sixteen thousand women being kept there against their will. The story does not need to describe more than that for the wrongness to be clear.
The doors were opened. That is the victory, and it is not the sort that gets painted.
And then there is a question in the middle of this story that most stories would leave out.
Where were sixteen thousand women supposed to go?
Not home. Not in that world. Everybody they had come from would have looked at where they had been and decided something about them, and there would have been nowhere for any of them to stand.
So Kṛṣṇa married all of them.

This is not told as a romance. In that society, marriage gave the women a home and standing when returning to their earlier lives was no longer open to them. It was a response to an injustice, not a reward for it.
Then comes the part remembered by the festival.

Naraka was somebody's son. His mother is the earth herself, and she was there, and she did not argue that he had been good, because he had not been. She asked for one thing: that his boy be left alone. And she was listened to, on the field, immediately.
And she got more than she asked. The kingdom went to the boy — the same throne, the same city, handed over on the field the morning his father died on it.
And then he asked for something.

Festival tradition says Naraka did not ask to live or to be forgiven. He asked that when people remembered this day, they should not keep it only as the day he was beaten. They should light lamps, give things to each other, and be glad.
That later tradition is why the fourteenth night of the waning fortnight is remembered as Naraka Chaturdaśī, kept every year in the name of the man who lost.
The earrings went back to the old woman they had been taken from, which was what the whole journey had been for, and which by then nobody was thinking about.
The lamps on that night are his idea. He asked for a festival on the one day of the year that was always going to be about him losing, and he got it, and we are still keeping it.

linked.reason: the other night of lamps, two days later, and a completely different reason for lighting them

close.question: He could have asked for anything at the end. He asked that people be happy on the day he lost. Why do you think that was what he wanted?
close.seed: How a day gets remembered is sometimes the last thing anybody can choose.

ifTheyAsk.q: Why did Kṛṣṇa marry sixteen thousand women?
ifTheyAsk.a: Not for love, and the book does not pretend otherwise. In that world a woman who had been in Naraka's house could not go home — her family would not have taken her, and she would have had no standing anywhere. Marriage was the only arrangement that gave her one. It is worth saying plainly to an older child that this is a solution to an injustice, not a happy ending, and that the injustice is the part to be angry about.

ifTheyAsk.q: Is the last bit really in the book?
ifTheyAsk.a: No, and that is worth knowing. The Bhāgavata has the war, the earrings, the women and his mother. The dying request — lamps rather than mourning — is the festival's own story, told wherever Naraka Chaturdaśī is kept, rather than a verse anyone can point at. It is the reason the day has the shape it has, and it arrived after the book did.

ifTheyAsk.q: Why do people say Diwali is about Rāma, then?
ifTheyAsk.a: Because two stories settled on the same few nights, and where you grew up decides which one you were told. In the south the festival is the fourteenth — Naraka Chaturdaśī, kept before sunrise with an oil bath — and Naraka is the story. Further north the big night is the new moon after it, and the story is Rāma coming home, with Lakṣmī. Neither is a corruption of the other. And they are genuinely an age apart: Rāma belongs to the Tretā Yuga and Kṛṣṇa to the Dvāpara, landing on adjoining nights of the same month. Whether the festival gathered them because the dates matched, or the dates are remembered that way because it gathered them, nobody can say.
